description: I build ML pipelines on real Earth observation data and care a lot about getting the science right: uncertainty, validation, and whether a result actually holds up. I'm most interested in atmospheric and Earth science, and in turning huge, messy NASA datasets into things normal people can see and use.
summary: Sway creates stories about moving ground from NASA-ISRO NISAR radar data. Designed for Dancing with the SARs, it provides a tour of eight sites in five countries, a world map of 27 candidate detections from 137 checked locations, and an earthquake game where visitors fit a fault to real radar observations. In Mexico City we merge radar, population and transport maps to estimate who and what is on moving ground. We show all eleven predefined tests: seven passed and four failed. The measurements are along the radar viewing direction, not necessarily vertical motion. Sources, methods and the AI investigator’s transcripts are public. Sway lets you explore satellite measurements with the limitations in view.
details:
It’s hard to notice movement of the ground in daily life. Sway makes it something for people to explore: a sinking city, a sliding hillside, the surface pattern left behind by an earthquake. A 60-second tour introduces eight case studies from five countries. The World map widens the search with NISAR observations from July to October 2026. Of 137 locations with usable checks we kept 27 candidate motion detections, showed 100 with nothing detectable, and excluded 10 whose patterns we could not confidently tie to the target feature. A quiet result means that this method did not detect movement in that window; it does not prove that the ground is at rest.

Mexico City brings the stakes home. On the radar map we superimpose the GHS-POP 2025 population grid and the OpenStreetMap infrastructure. An estimated 3.3 million people live in areas that are moving more than 10 cm/year away from the satellite and about 17 of the 20 km of Metro Line B that fall within the radar footprint intersect those areas. These are estimates of population and infrastructure overlapping measured motion, not counts of damaged buildings or people at risk. Thresholds are based on radar-direction motion. Interpreting these as vertical sinking rates requires assumptions about the direction of movement.

We fit a rectangular fault model to earthquake radar patterns in Japan and Panama, and compare the results with USGS catalog measurements. The Japan model was successful in all three pre-defined tests. Panama passed one and failed two, even though its model explained 97% of the variation in the radar picture. That contrast matters: a close visual match does not guarantee a correct physical explanation. The Earthquake game gives visitors the same model to play with. They drag and tweak a fault, see its predicted pattern cancel out parts of the observed signal, and compare their fit with the computer’s.

Sway uses NISAR Level-2 geocoded unwrapped interferograms, a provisional product provided by ASF DAAC, as its starting point. Our Python pipeline finds scenes through NASA’s Common Metadata Repository and reads the data covering each study area. It filters out poor-quality pairs, applies the supplied ionosphere and atmospheric corrections, then combines consecutive observations on the native 80-metre grid. The website displays the processed measurements using MapLibre and deck.gl. Sway calculates local time series, model fits and exposure estimates, and provides interactive views; it does not generate the original NISAR interferograms. Measurements show motion toward or away from the satellite relative to reference ground, though sideways movement can also influence the reading.

We published eleven tests before running the analyses they evaluate. Seven passed; four failed. The tests weren’t all blind: we had already inspected calibration data, and we knew the earthquake catalogue values before finalizing the second test set. At Oak Ridge, the radar detected the moving landslide strip but didn’t match GPS measurements of its magnitude. We present that failure alongside the result. A quiet result does not rule out motion too small or too spatially smooth for this method to detect. The provisional data and experimental processing aren’t suitable for building-level safety decisions.

An AI investigator examines the measurements using read-only tools, checks the view from the other direction and weighs alternative explanations. It flagged Guadalupe Landfill as a low-confidence lead that may be consistent with settlement, though the cause hasn’t been confirmed. Reports link to the tool results and full transcripts. An automated check confirms that reported numbers appear in the cited tool outputs. This can catch misquotations, but it can’t validate the scientific conclusions.

Sway is for curious residents, students and educators who want to learn what radar can reveal. The tour offers a starting point, the game gives people room to experiment, and the evidence pages invite them to question the results. We hope it makes ground-motion science easier to discuss and explore. The project uses Python, NumPy, SciPy, h5py, fsspec, pyproj, rasterio, Shapely, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, deck.gl and Vercel.

AI assistance

The team selected the challenge and shaped the project around showing how ground motion affects people and places. Anthropic Claude and OpenAI Codex helped brainstorm features, find research sources, analyze results, design the interface, write most of the code, and draft the text. AI assistants also helped create the script for the screen-recorded demo. The app includes an AI investigator, and its tool calls and reports are made public. QuillBot and Ahrefs helped refine the submission wording, which was then reviewed for clarity and accuracy. The demo shows the working website and contains no synthetic people, generated images, speech, or music. NISAR provides the radar observations; our analysis turns them into derived maps and model estimates.
